item.title: Africa's Cities Are Growing Faster Than Their Plans. That Might Not Be a Disaster.
item.description:
The standard way of talking about African urban growth is a warning.

Cities expanding faster than roads can be built or pipes can be laid. Housing shortages that push millions into informal settlements. Traffic that turns short distances into long ordeals. Flooding in neighbourhoods that were built without drainage because nobody planned for them at all.

These are real problems. Anyone who has spent time in a rapidly growing African city knows them directly.

item.title: Africa's Youth Is Not a Problem. It's the Point.
item.description:
Every few months, a new report comes out about Africa’s growing youth population.

The language is nearly always the same. Words like “challenge,” “pressure,” and “risk” show up early. The concern is built around jobs, stability, and the strain that a large young population puts on systems that were not built with them in mind.

The concern is real. But the framing is wrong — and it keeps getting in the way of a more honest conversation.

item.title: In Defence of Reading Slowly
item.description:
There is a certain satisfaction in finishing a book.

Closing the last page, adding the title to a list, moving on to the next one. It feels like progress — measured, visible, building up over time. Many readers track how many books they get through in a year and feel a quiet sense of accomplishment when the number grows.

The trouble is that reading a book and absorbing a book are not always the same thing.

item.title: Mobile Money Changed Everything. Here's What Comes Next.
item.description:
When M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007, most of the global finance world did not pay much attention.

A mobile money service for a developing market. Useful, perhaps, for people without bank accounts. But not exactly the kind of thing that turns heads in London or New York.

What followed surprised almost everyone.

Within a few years, millions of Kenyans who had never held a bank account were sending money, paying bills, and setting aside savings — all through a basic mobile phone. Research later showed that M-Pesa helped lift a measurable share of Kenyan households out of poverty by giving people, and women in particular, a new kind of economic independence.

item.title: The Drum Major Is Gone: A Tribute to Reverend Jesse Louis Jackson
item.description: There are people who arrive in the world as if they were sent with a specific assignment. They do not drift through history — they shape it. They do not ask permission to speak — they thunder. Reverend Jesse Louis Jackson was one of those people. Born October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, a city that taught him injustice before it taught him anything else, he left this world on February 17, 2026, at the age of 84 — peacefully, surrounded by family, in Chicago, the city he made his pulpit and his battlefield.

item.title: The Forgotten Art of Finishing Things
item.description:
There is a certain kind of folder that lives on almost every creative person’s computer.

It goes by different names — “drafts,” “ideas,” “in progress” — but the contents are always more or less the same. A half-written piece that seemed important at the time. An unfinished project from a year or two ago. A voice note with an idea that felt urgent and never went anywhere. Things that were started with real energy and quietly set aside.

item.title: The Problem Is Not That People Don't Read. It's What They're Reading.
item.description:
Every so often, a new study or column appears warning that people are reading less.

Attention spans are shrinking. Books are losing ground. Long-form journalism is struggling to survive. The concern is framed as a quantity problem: not enough reading is happening.

But watch what people actually do with their phones.

They read constantly. Captions. Threads. Comment sections. Group chats. Newsletters. Long arguments that play out over dozens of replies. People who say they do not read are often reading for several hours every day.

item.title: We Talk About Mental Health. We Don't Fund It.
item.description:
Something has shifted in the way people talk about mental health.

The conversations have become more open. In certain circles, the old silence has started to break down. Young people especially have been more willing to speak honestly — about anxiety, about burnout, about the strain of navigating economies that demand a great deal and offer little security in return.

This change matters. Language shapes how problems get understood. Naming something is the first step toward addressing it.

item.title: What Loss Teaches About the Value of Ordinary Time
item.description:
Grief does something strange to time.

Most people, before they experience real loss, think of time as moving in a straight line — the past behind, the future ahead, events receding in the rear-view as life pushes forward. And in a technical sense, time does keep moving that way. The calendar continues. The world around keeps going at its ordinary pace.

But inside, something different happens.

Certain moments stop behaving like the past and start feeling present. A voice. A laugh at a particular pitch. The quality of light in a room on an afternoon that seemed entirely ordinary until it became the last one. These moments do not recede the way they are supposed to. They come back, unbidden, and feel as close as this morning.

item.title: What the Yaytseslav Scandal Reveals About Kenya's Blind Spots
item.description:
By now, most Kenyans online know the name Yaytseslav.

A Russian national, also identified as Vyacheslav Trahov, spent time in Kenya — and Ghana — approaching women in malls, on streets, and in supermarkets. He struck up conversations, collected phone numbers, arranged private meetups, and secretly filmed the encounters. The footage was then shared on TikTok, Instagram, and Telegram to an audience that treated it as entertainment.

When the videos spread widely across Kenyan social media last week, the reaction was swift. The Ministry of Gender condemned the acts. Security agencies were directed to trace and arrest the man. Ghana’s government announced it would seek cooperation from Moscow through diplomatic channels. The word “exploitation” appeared in official statements. The word “violation” appeared in many more.

item.title: Why We Stopped Being Bored — and What We Lost
item.description:
There used to be a moment on public transport that almost everyone knew.

You sat down. You had nothing in your hands. Your eyes drifted to the window, and your mind went somewhere — a half-formed thought, an old memory, a question that had been sitting at the back of your head for days. Nobody asked for that moment. It just happened.

Today, that moment barely gets a chance to show up.

item.title: Living With Constant Information Noise
item.description:
There was a time when silence was normal.

You could sit somewhere and your mind would simply… rest. Thoughts came and went on their own. Curiosity existed, but it wasn’t constantly triggered. You learned things, but learning had edges — it started and it stopped.

Today, that boundary is gone.

From the moment we wake up, information rushes in. Notifications before we even get out of bed. Messages, headlines, videos, opinions, updates. Even when we are not actively looking for information, it finds us anyway.

item.title: Welcome to this new corner of the internet
item.description:
Welcome to Veridus, a fresh home for exploration and shared discovery. We built this digital space for anyone who finds themselves fascinated by the intersection of modern technology and mindful living. Our goal is to move beyond the surface level, offering a hub where curiosity leads to genuine inspiration for readers from every walk of life.

Tech, Culture, and Everything Between

If you are a tech enthusiast, you will find deep dives into Linux tips, ethical hacking insights, and the software trends currently defining our digital landscape. We believe technology is best understood when paired with a human perspective. That is why we also explore the vibrant world of culture and creativity. From time-honored traditions and literature to the diverse stories that make our world unique, we aim to celebrate the arts in all their forms.

item.title: Why Nairobi Is the Capital of Africa
item.description:
Nairobi is not officially the capital of Africa. There is no declaration, no charter, no continental vote that says so. Addis Ababa holds that title on paper, and rightly so. But capitals are not only decided by documents. Some are shaped by movement, energy, and influence. And by that measure, Nairobi has quietly become something more — not by force, not by announcement, but by gravity.

One way to see a city’s influence is to watch where people go. Nairobi draws people from all over Africa — students, journalists, artists, activists, freelancers, and dreamers. Some arrive with clear plans. Many arrive unsure of what lies ahead. Most come because Nairobi feels like possibility. People arrive seeking opportunities, connection, and a chance to grow. Writers come to find new stories. Musicians come to collaborate. Entrepreneurs come because the city’s energy inspires action. Nairobi doesn’t promise an easy path, but it gives people a sense that something can happen — that they can create, learn, and contribute. This is what gives Nairobi its pull. It’s not about perfection. It’s about the chance to be part of something bigger, to move, to meet others, and to leave a mark that goes beyond the city itself.

item.title: The Drawbacks of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly become part of everyday life. From recommendation systems and chatbots to medical diagnostics and autonomous vehicles, AI promises efficiency, speed, and innovation. However, despite its impressive capabilities, AI also comes with significant drawbacks that deserve careful attention. Ignoring these issues can lead to long-term social, economic, and ethical consequences.

One major drawback of AI is job displacement. As AI systems automate tasks once performed by humans, many traditional jobs are at risk. Roles in manufacturing, customer support, transportation, and even creative industries are increasingly being replaced or augmented by machines. While new jobs may emerge, the transition is often uneven, leaving many workers without the skills or resources needed to adapt. This can widen economic inequality and create social instability.

item.title: Digital Privacy in 2024: What You Need to Know Right Now
item.description:
Last year, I received a targeted advertisement for a specific ailment I’d never searched for, never mentioned online, and barely acknowledged to myself. I was genuinely unsettled. How did they know? The answer, once I started investigating, was more complex and more troubling than simple algorithmic inference. They knew because my data had been sold, traded, and analyzed by at least seven different companies I’d never directly interacted with.

That experience became the catalyst for understanding something I’d intellectually known but hadn’t emotionally grasped: your digital footprint is larger than you can probably imagine. Every app you download, every website you visit, every search you make—it’s being tracked, analyzed, combined with data from other sources, and sometimes sold to the highest bidder. In 2024, understanding digital privacy isn’t optional; it’s essential for maintaining autonomy over your own life.

item.title: The Future of AI in African Tech: Building Local Solutions
item.description: I remember the first time I understood that Africa’s tech future wouldn’t look like Silicon Valley’s past. It was at a startup pitch event in Nairobi three years ago, watching a young developer from Kisii present an AI system that could predict crop diseases from mobile phone images. The room fell silent—not because the technology was groundbreaking by global standards, but because it was built by someone who had spent their childhood watching their parents lose harvests to preventable diseases.

item.title: Remote Work Isn't the Future—It's a Privilege We Need to Redistribute
item.description:
I’ve watched something troubling unfold over the past few years. We celebrate remote work as liberation. Tech workers in my circle praise the flexibility, the commute savings, the ability to live literally anywhere. But this celebration masks a troubling reality that I can’t ignore: remote work has become a new form of inequality.

The narrative about remote work is overwhelmingly told by people who benefit from it. The software engineer who sold his Nairobi apartment and bought a bigger one in Mombasa. The designer who moved from Nairobi to a rural area, keeping her San Francisco salary. The consultant who negotiated flexible hours and now works from coffee shops three days a week. These stories are presented as inevitable and universal progress.

item.title: Why Nairobi Deserves to Be the Cultural Capital of East Africa
item.description:
There’s a prevailing narrative that Cairo is the cultural capital of Africa. Or that Lagos represents the creative heartbeat of the continent. But I would argue—passionately—that Nairobi, my home, and increasingly the epicenter of East African culture, deserves equal recognition. Not because it’s trying to be like the others. Because it’s becoming something entirely its own.

I grew up in Nairobi in the 1990s, when it was regarded internationally as primarily a political capital and safari gateway. But something has shifted fundamentally in the last fifteen years. Walk through neighborhoods like Westlands, Karen, or South B today and you’ll encounter something remarkable: a genuinely cosmopolitan creative scene that draws from the city’s incredibly diverse populations while maintaining a distinct identity that feels authentically Nairobi.

item.title: The Digital Detox Guide: How to Reclaim Your Attention (Without Going Off-Grid)
item.description:
I watch my phone buzz and I check it without thinking. Three minutes later, I’ve somehow lost forty-five minutes to scrolling—not because I wanted to, but because the app kept feeding me content designed specifically to keep me scrolling. This pattern repeats a dozen times daily. I’m not unique. Most people reading this will recognize this exact experience.

Here’s what I’ve learned through investigation and genuine struggle: you’re not weak. You’re not lacking discipline. You’re fighting against technology that employs thousands of people specifically to make it addictive. That’s not a fair fight.

item.title: Africa's Renewable Energy Boom: Why the Continent Could Lead the World
item.description: I spent a week in rural Kenya last year, staying with a family that lives completely off-grid powered by solar panels the size of a small window. The mother of the household told me something I haven’t been able to shake: “For the first time in my life, I don’t have to think about energy.” She wasn’t using a generator that requires fuel she has to drive to town to buy. She wasn’t relying on an electrical grid that might fail for weeks. She had sunlight—which is abundantly free—converted into electricity.

item.title: A Beginner's Guide to Sustainable Living in the City
item.description:
I used to feel genuinely anxious about environmental impact. The statistics are overwhelming—climate change accelerating, plastic choking oceans, biodiversity collapsing. I’d read articles about zero-waste living, pristine compost systems, perfect environmental choices, and feel paralyzed. How could I possibly do enough?

Then something shifted. I realized the narrative around sustainable living was designed by people with enormous privilege. Those Instagram accounts showing perfect minimalist homes, beautiful compost bins, and flawless environmental footprints? Those people usually had resources I didn’t have. But more importantly, I was approaching sustainability wrong.

item.title: Why Free Online Education Hasn't Solved Inequality—And What Might
item.description:
I believed in the promise. When massive open online courses (MOOCs) first appeared, I genuinely thought we were witnessing an educational revolution. Free lectures from world-class professors at elite universities. Anyone with internet access could learn quantum physics from MIT or economics from Stanford. YouTube became an infinite classroom. The narrative was compelling: information asymmetry was solved. Education was being democratized.

Yet here I am, years later, watching educational inequality persist and even deepen. Not because online education failed. But because we fundamentally misunderstood what education actually is.

item.title: The Art of the Simple Dinner: Building a Weeknight Cooking Practice
item.description:
I stood in my kitchen last month looking at a recipe promising “30 minutes.” I started cooking. An hour later, I’d burned something, forgotten an ingredient I didn’t have, and spent three times what takeout would have cost. I ordered pizza. Again.

This is a pattern I lived for years. Cooking felt impossible. Too time-consuming, too complicated, too likely to fail. The safer option was outsourcing meals. And if you spend more than ten minutes in any urban center, you know outsourcing is always available.

item.title: How African Cities Are Solving Urban Problems With Grassroots Innovation
item.description: I was stuck in Lagos traffic for four hours last month—which isn’t unusual, but this time I was sitting next to a founder who was solving the problem I was experiencing. She was on a call about an app that coordinates shared electric vehicles for last-mile transportation. Meanwhile, the woman in front of me was struggling with plastic waste, a problem being tackled by a startup converting that waste into building materials. The traffic caused me frustration; it caused these entrepreneurs to see opportunity.

item.title: About Veridus

Veridus is an independent news review publication dedicated to making sense of the world’s most important stories. We dig into the headlines, provide context, and offer clear-eyed analysis of events unfolding across the globe.

The name Veridus is rooted in truth — and that is the standard we hold ourselves to.

What we cover

We review and analyse news across politics, culture, technology, and society. Rather than simply reporting what happened, we ask why it matters and what it means — for your community, your country, and the world.
